newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian opposition adds to Prodi's woes on Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italian opposition adds to Prodi's woes on Albania.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government faced the embarrassing prospect on Tuesday of having to vote for an opposition motion to ensure the deployment of an Italian-led multinational force in Albania.

With his own parliamentary majority in tatters on the issue, Prime Minister Romano Prodi had banked on centre-right Freedom Alliance backing in votes in parliament to secure endorsement of the first such mission to be led by Italy.

But the main opposition bloc declared after a meeting of its parties' leaders that it would vote 'no' to a government resolution on the mission, due to deploy some time next week with up to 6,000 troops from as many as eight nations.
Freedom Alliance leader Silvio Berlusconi said his bloc supported the mission but wanted its own motion to pass.
"I don't see why the Olive Tree (governing coalition) should not vote for our motion. All criticism of the government has been eliminated from it," Berlusconi said.
Prodi's government has a majority in the Senate (upper house), where a vote on the mission was due on Tuesday.

However, it cannot win a similar vote on its own resolution on Wednesday in the lower Chamber of Deputies, where the government's parliamentary ally Communist Refoundation led by Marxist Fausto Bertinotti holds the balance of power.
It opposes the force and has said it will vote 'no' in both houses, placing severe strain on the partnership with Prodi and the 11-month-old government's longer term prospects.

"The government is exposed. Berlusconi is calling the shots thanks to Bertinotti's incomprehensible and irresponsible position," said Massimo D'Alema, leader of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the biggest in the government.

It was not immediately clear how the coalition would resolve its dilemma but unless it backs the opposition motion in the Chamber, it risks a defeat that would put considerable pressure on Prodi to resign.

"Given that the (government) majority doesn't exist any more, they could easily swing their votes behind our motion which clearly says 'yes' to the mission," said Gianfranco Fini, whose hard-right National Alliance is part of Berlusconi's bloc.

The Freedom Alliance altered its stance after a prominent member of the government, deputy foreign minister Piero Fassino of the PDS, declared in public that Italy believed Albania's embattled President Sali Berisha should leave office.
"That Berisha should go is very clear, at least to us. And when I say us I'm not just talking about the PDS, I'm also talking about the government," Fassino told a PDS meeting.
Fassino said that Berisha should not step down now because his departure might spark the fall of Albania's new national unity government, led by opposition Socialist Bashkim Fino.
Fassino later sought to clarify his remarks and Prodi told reporters that "I do not want to interfere in the internal politics of Albania".
But Fassino's comments nonetheless enraged the opposition, which has political links with Berisha's Democratic Party.
"Things like this expose our boys (soldiers) to greater risks" in Albania, Berlusconi said.

Berisha, in office since 1992, has said he will resign if his party loses early general elections due to take place by the end of June under a broad political agreement reached last month to try to end his Balkan country's anarchy.

Rebel committees holding southern Albanian towns have called for Berisha's immediate resignation, accusing him of failure to control shady investment schemes that collapsed with the life savings of tens of thousands of people.
